results.title: Colombia: Flash Update 006 - Update on the Impact of the Earthquake in Colombia - August 14, 2026
results.description: Country: Colombia Sources: El Equipo Humanitario País Colombia, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached file. This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia in collaboration with humanitarian partners, based on official reports (as of 14 August, 18:30 local time). The next update to this document will be issued on Monday, 17 August 2026. Humanitarian impact and multisectoral effects. Five days after the magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, 183 aftershocks have been reported, along with impacts across 15 departments and 437 municipalities. At least 135,179 people have been affected, including Afro-Colombian and Indigenous communities, while significant damage to housing, critical infrastructure and essential services persists. Priority needs and scaling up of the response. The most pressing needs remain in health, temporary shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), food security, energy and communications, particularly in Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó and Caldas departments. Rapid and intersectoral assessments are ongoing to identify gaps, prioritize interventions and complement the Government's response in the most affected areas. International support mobilization and humanitarian coordination. The international response continues to scale up, with an initial allocation of US$5 million from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), additional donor contributions and the operational deployment of national and international humanitarian partners. Efforts are focused on strengthening immediate response capacity, restoring essential services and supporting early recovery in coordination with the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) and territorial authorities.

results.title: 'Never seen corruption of this magnitude': Horror as Trump family closer to launching bank
results.description: The Trump family's pathway to opening a bank through its cryptocurrency investments is sending shockwaves, according to reporting by the Wall Street Journal. A trust company for World Liberty Financial , the Trump family's flagship crypto venture, has preliminary conditional approval to become a bank, The Journal reported. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, a Treasury bureau, gave the early preliminary approval on Friday. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) wrote in a statement that "we have never seen financial conflicts or corruption of this magnitude." President Donald Trump and his two sons launched World Liberty in late 2024 but have not yet made available promised borrowing, lending, and trading services, according to The Journal. If World Liberty Trust secures final approval, it will be able to operate as a federally chartered national trust bank, which will allow it to issue, redeem, and safeguard a dollar-backed stablecoin it launched last year, The Journal reported. The stablecoin has a market value of about $4 billion, according to The Journal. Unlike full banks, trust banks generally can't take deposits or make loans, The Journal reported. However, Trump has reported $1.4 billion in earnings from his memecoin and crypto ventures. The Journal noted that those earnings are "the biggest roadblock" for the Clarity Act, a landmark bill seeking a comprehensive regulatory framework for digital assets. The White House has previously defended Trump's financial ventures as president, saying "neither the President nor his family has ever engaged—or will ever engage—in conflicts of interest," according to The Journal. Zach Witkoff, the son of the president's friend and Middle East envoy, Steve Witkoff , is the chief executive of World Liberty Financial and chairman of World Liberty Trust Company. The company said it submitted "probably one of the most thoroughly reviewed applications in the history of the OCC" to become a bank, according to The Journal. "We answered all of the regulator's questions, and we accepted the significant obligations and ongoing scrutiny that come with the national charter," Zach Witkoff said in an interview, per The Journal. "If we were looking for less oversight, we would not have chosen federal supervision."
